title: Customer sidecar augmentation patterns for safe IaC upgrades
creator: Ava Kapoor
description: Problem: Customers require small, tenant-specific tweaks to our Private (VPC) Terraform bundles (e.g., extra security group rules, bespoke DNS records, nonstandard IAM roles). Forking core modules per customer explodes maintenance and makes upgrades dangerous. We need a composable pattern that lets ops/solutions engineers apply per-customer customizations without copying core modules, and that provides safe upgrade paths with automated preflight checks and post-upgrade health verification.
proposed_solution:
Introduce a lightweight 'tenant-sidecar' augmentation pattern: a thin wrapper module that composes core modules and a customer overlay module. The wrapper merges customer-provided overlay objects with well-defined extension points (locals + merge for maps, concat for lists) and exposes only a controlled set of override hooks (network_rules, route_overrides, extra_tags, provider_aliases). Key elements:
- keep core modules immutable and versioned (module source + tag).
- expose a fixed augmentation surface: augment_inputs (map), augment_modules (list of module rebinds), and preflight_hooks (external scripts).
- use terraform 'for_each' on a tenants map in the deployment driver to instantiate sidecars per-tenant.
- perform pre-apply plan validations via CI (terraform plan + custom linter) and a lightweight policy checker (OPA/sentinel-style script) that can block or warn on risky changes (eg. changing subnets, KMS keys).
- implement post-apply health checks executed via orchestration job (k8s/CICD runner) that exercise runbook endpoints (control-plane /health, test inference path, KV cache warmup) and publish results to Console dashboard.
- keep secrets and customer-sensitive overrides in a controlled secret-store (KMS/HashiCorp Vault) referenced by ID in overlays rather than in plaintext in overlays.
design_decisions:
- Do NOT allow arbitrary module source overrides in overlays; only allow parameter-level augmentation and well-known extension modules.
- Use object/map merging (local merged = merge(var.core_defaults, var.customer_overrides)) as the canonical merge pattern rather than string patching.
- Provider aliasing: customer sidecars may need provider aliases (eg. aws.customer) — sidecar supports passing provider_config aliases and wiring them into child modules via providers = { aws = aws.customer }.
- Plan-time validation: add a 'preflight' job that runs terraform plan and two validators: (1) diff-rules that detect destructive network/iam changes, (2) cost-estimator for obvious quota/cost spikes.
- Upgrade safety: pin core module versions and implement canary upgrades by applying new module versions to a small set of tenants via the deployment driver flags before broad rollouts.
- Health checks are idempotent and have timeouts; failures mark the tenant upgrade as failed and trigger automatic rollback instructions (not automatic rollbacks in first phase).
acceptance_criteria: A tenant-sidecar wrapper module exists in our modules repo and is consumed by the private-deploy driver.
Overlay merge semantics are documented and unit-tested (map/list merging behaviours).
CI preflight job rejects overlays that attempt to replace module sources or change pinned-provider aliases without security approval.
A staged canary upgrade for module v2.0 has been executed against 3 staging tenants with green health checks recorded in Console.
An operator runbook exists: how to add a new customer overlay, how to run preflight locally, and how to interpret post-apply health failures.

rollout_plan: Phase 1 (internal staging): validate pattern on non-customer staging tenants. Phase 2 (pilot customers): migrate 2 small customers to sidecar approach with manual review. Phase 3 (canary upgrades): apply module upgrades to 5 pilot customers and run extended health checks for 48h. Phase 4 (general availability): flip driver flag to allow all new private deployments to use sidecar augmentation; provide migration tooling for existing customer overlays.
test_plan:
- Unit tests: terratest/inspec for module outputs and merge logic.
- CI plan-only: terraform init + terraform plan for each overlay against a mock tenant state to ensure no unexpected resource replacements.
- Policy tests: run OPA policies that assert no changes to protected resources (primary KMS key ARNs, core VPC cidr) unless explicit 'security_exemption' approved.
- Post-apply health: automated script that calls control-plane /health, a short inference path with synthetic payload, and checks tokenized cost meter. Results must be green before marking tenant upgrade successful.
- Failure scenarios: simulate overlay that attempts to widen CIDR; CI must block and provide remediation hints.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Overly permissive overlays could introduce security changes. Mitigation: enforce policy checks and require security approval for any overlay that touches protected keys/resources.
Risk: Merge ambiguity for list concatenation causing duplicate SG rules. Mitigation: canonicalize lists (unique by rule-id) during merge and provide lint warnings.
Risk: Secrets leakage in overlays. Mitigation: only secret references (secret_id) allowed in overlays; CI rejects literal secrets; provide docs for Vault/KMS usage.
Risk: Upgrades causing downtime. Mitigation: canary + health checks + automated rollback playbook (manual rollback first phase).
notes:
- This pattern is intentionally conservative: first-class goal is to reduce forks and make upgrades predictable.
- Avoid feature creep: do not add arbitrary templating languages in overlays in this phase.
- Follow-on work: explore an interactive overlay validation UI in Console so non-technical customers can preview changes.
approvals: Security review kickoff scheduled 2025-02-20. Engineering signoff required after canary.
followups: - Expand preflight policy set with more cost heuristics. - Add a scoped auto-rollback experiment after manual confidence increases.
